video_title: Circle Episode 04 | Dream | Subtitles | 23rd October 2026 | Hina Tariq & Khaqan Shahnawaz | Green TV
comment:
Thank you for raising such an important issue concerning Pakistan’s collapsing healthcare system.

We, the young doctors who form the backbone of this country's healthcare system, are facing one of the worst professional crises imaginable. Young doctors, including House Officers and postgraduate trainees, are forced to work 36 hour consecutive shifts, often for salaries (Rs. 50k - Rs. 70k) that barely reflect the hours they put in or the responsibilities they carry. It is shameful that even security guards working 8–12-hour shifts in the same hospitals can earn salaries comparable to those of young doctors working around the clock. This is not meant to undermine the work of security personnel, but to highlight just how poorly our healthcare professionals are compensated.

A person who has been working continuously for over 30 hours cannot reasonably be expected to function at their best, particularly during the final hours of such an exhausting shift. And when you're dealing with human lives, the consequences of exhaustion can be devastating. The working conditions are equally pathetic. Many hospitals do not even have proper doctors' lounges or designated resting areas where doctors can take a short break during these inhumane shifts. Consequently, exhausted doctors sometimes fall asleep at their desks or workstations whenever they get a few moments of rest. Instead of understanding the circumstances, patient attendants often record videos of these doctors and circulate them on social media, portraying them as irresponsible professionals who are neglecting their duties. Many attendants bring expired patients and resort to violence on doctors when bad news gets broken to them as if doctors had killed them

What makes matters worse is that hospital administrations and the government repeatedly make doctors the scapegoats for their own administrative failures and shortcomings. Our healthcare system is stretched beyond its limits. Doctors in Pakistan often shoulder workloads 5 times more than those of their counterparts in Europe, while earning only a fraction of what doctors in developed countries are paid. The expectations are enormous, the compensation is miserable, and the working conditions are downright inhumane.

The irony is that Pakistan does not necessarily have a shortage of qualified doctors. It has a severe shortage of adequately equipped hospitals, funded positions, and employment opportunities for those doctors. Thousands of qualified medical graduates struggle to find suitable jobs while existing hospitals remain overcrowded and understaffed. This is a failure of healthcare planning and governance.

Moreover, I would like to point out a few factual inaccuracies in the episode regarding the USMLE. The USMLE is not a pen and paper examination. It is a computer-based examination series consisting of three steps, with Step 1 and Step 2 CK each lasting approximately eight and nine hours, respectively. The entire process certainly does not cost just Rs. 800,000. Each step carries a separate examination fee. Then there are the expenses associated with clinical electives, US clinical experience, visa applications, travelling, accommodation, ECFMG certification, and numerous other costs totalling Rs. 7-8 million. Even applying for a single residency Match cycle can cost over Rs. 1 million, depending on the number of programmes applied to and the circumstances of the applicant. For many Pakistani graduates, the overall financial burden can run into several million rupees.

The system is deeply flawed, and unfortunately, it is the young doctors who bear the consequences of its failures. We spend years competing in one of the toughest academic environments, sacrifice our youth studying and training, and enter this profession as some of the brightest students in the country, only to face unemployment, exploitation, exhaustion, and a complete lack of professional dignity. And then we wonder why so many talented young doctors are desperate to leave Pakistan. The real tragedy is not that our doctors want to leave. The real tragedy is that our system gives them so few reasons to stay!

comment:
No matter what, Zarrena is right from her own perspective. She knew nothing about Balla’s past during their marriage. She married him, and everything seemed to be going well until Balla decided to take revenge on Billo. That was when Zarrena discovered the truth about his past, but even then, she chose to stay with him.

The very next day, she found out that her husband was a murderer, and suddenly, she had to face the loss of her home, her family, her brother, and Balla himself.

Balla may have provided her with money and a house, but he failed to give her the emotional support, love, and honesty she deserved. He never truly accepted his mistakes or shared the truth about his past with her. A relationship cannot survive on material things alone; it also needs trust, honesty, and emotional security.

That’s why Zarrena is justified in her own position. She was a wife who trusted her husband, but she ended up suffering the consequences of choices she never made.

Apart from all this, Wahaj Ali’s acting is absolutely outstanding. He has portrayed Balla’s character brilliantly. But appreciating Wahaj Ali as an actor doesn’t mean we have to justify Balla’s actions. Balla may be brilliantly portrayed, but he was wrong in the way he treated his wife. Zarrena deserved the truth, love, and emotional support that Balla failed to give her.
